INTRODUCTIONM
During flight, many of the aircraft's systems are used at the same time. If one of the systems malfunctions or fails, the aircraft could perform poorly or crash.
To ensure the safety of the aircraft and its passengers, the pilot is required to continuously monitor the status of all flight operations................

This lesson introduces you to the aircraft master warning and annunciator system. You will see how the pilot is able to monitor the status of all flight operations and still be able to pay attention to where the aircraft is going...
Let's begin the lesson on MASTER WARNING AND ANNUNCIATOR SYSTEM.............

DISCUSSION
The purpose of the master warning and annunciator system is to alert and inform the pilot of the aircraft's condition.
Each individual operational system of the aircraft has a fault indicator light located on the overhead panel or fire module.
In contrast, the master warning and annunciator system lights are located on the forward panel in front of the pilot and copilot for easy visibility.
OVERHEAD

When an operational system malfunctions, that system's fault indicator illuminates on the overhead panel. Additionally, the appropriate Master Caution, Fire Warn, and annunciator lights illuminate directly in the pilot's field of vision...
Illumination of the Master Caution or Fire Warning annunciators alert the pilot and copilot to check the system fault indicators on the overhead panel.
INVERTER
R IGNITION ON
PASS OXY ON
R BL AIR OFF
L GEN OVHT

Each aircraft manufacturer and type of aircraft may use a different design and layout for the indicator system, but the purpose remains the same: to inform the pilots of system malfunctions and status...
All manufacturers follow a standard color coding for indicator lights. This ensures the pilot understands the severity of the indications.
Warning lights are red in color and alert the pilot and copilot of dangerous conditions. For example, generator failure is considered to be a flight-threatening condition.

Caution lights are yellow and indicate abnormal conditions. These conditions are not considered hazardous to the aircraft's flight. For example, if the Inertial Navigational System (INS) were failing, the aircraft could remain airborne...
Indicators and advisory lights reflect normal conditions or positions. Sometimes these lights are located on the annunciator panel.
Indicators and advisory lights are green, blue, and white in color.
Some manufacturers may use only one or two of these colors.
OVERHEAD
Two Master Caution lights are located in direct view of the pilot and copilot for quick recognition of an alarm indicator that has been set due to a faulty system.
Depending on the manufacturer, these lights may be red or yellow in color and may be labeled as Master Caution or Master Warning.

The system may be equipped with an audible alarm, such as a buzzer. Larger aircraft are normally equipped with buzzers because the pilot has more indicators and controls to monitor than in smaller aircraft...
After recognizing a fault, either the pilot or the copilot can extinguish both indicators by pressing the Master Caution light on the forward panel in view.?
The annunciator panel helps the pilot or copilot identify the faulty system at a glance. Then individual caution lights for the faulty system can be investigated.
These annunciator panels are designed as general system indicators. This means the pilot or copilot looks at another system panel associated with the illuminated annunciator to isolate a problem...
For example, the annunciator panel may have an indicator labeled Doors. If this indicator were illuminated, the pilot or copilot would check another panel to see which door is open.
FWD CABIN
FUEL PRESSURE

Some annunciator panels have specific system items labeled and color coded. In this case, additional annunciator lights are not necessary. This enables the pilot and copilot to see specific system faults immediately...

Individual system lights are usually located on the overhead panel. They are not readily visible to the pilot and copilot.
The annunciator uses several types of electrical switches and relays to indicate a fault.
FWD CABIN
FUEL PRESSURE
Micro-switches are used to indicate a position of a system component, such as a door or landing gear.
Relays are used for electrical flow indications, such as the loss of generators. They are also used with other switches to aid in the resetting of the annunciator circuit.

Thermal-switches are used to activate the circuit when a specific temperature is reached in a system or component. A Thermal Switch may be used for the compartment heater temperature circuit. If the temperature is too high, the annunciator is lit...
FUEL PRESSURE
Pressure switches are used to activate the annunciator when a system's pressure is not within normal operating parameters. The aircraft hydraulic system uses this type of switch.
Simple series and parallel circuits are used to illuminate and extinguish the annunciator panel. Each manufacturer uses different circuit configurations to achieve the same results.
A door warning circuit could be designed as the one shown. When a door is opened, the switch closes, completing the path for current. The appropriate indicators are illuminated.
When a door is opened, a path to ground is provided, making the circuit complete.
Integrity switches can be added so the pilot and copilot can determine which door is open or selectively check each door's position.

A completely different type of door warning circuit is the Door Advisory circuit. It is a series circuit which illuminates a green indicator when all the doors are closed. When one door opens, the path for current is broken and the indicator is extinguished...
COPILOT M/C
MASTER WARNING
FUEL PRESS
Most systems use SCRs (Silicon Controlled Rectifiers) to provide a path to ground when a system indicator is activated.
MASTER WARNING
When an aircraft system fault occurs, the printed circuit card (system sensor) provides the current needed to activate the SCR. This provides a path to ground for the appropriate warning light...
Momentarily pressing the Master Warning light removes power from and deactivates the SCR. The Master Warning light is then turned off with the loss of a path to ground.
The individual system light remains illuminated until the fault is corrected.
MASTER WARNING
If the fault remains, the pilot can press the Master Warning light to reactivate the SCR and illuminate the faulty system's annunciator.
If the system fault has been corrected, the power is removed from the SCR with the Master Warning light. The warning light does not clear automatically.
FUEL PRESS
Only the individual system indicator lights automatically reset after the fault is corrected.
This completes the information on MASTER WARNING AND ANNUNCIATOR SYSTEM.
1. The warning and annunciator system is placed within the normal view of the pilots, ensuring the pilots do not miss the indication.
2. All manufacturers follow a standard color coding for indicator lights. This ensures the pilot understands the severity of the indications.
3. Warning lights are red in color and alert the crew of dangerous operations or conditions. Generator failure is considered a hazardous condition.
4. Caution lights are yellow in color and indicate abnormal conditions that are not considered dangerous. Loss of INS (Inertial Navigation System) is considered an abnormal condition...
5. Depending on the manufacturer, indicator and advisory lights may be located on the annunciator panel. These lights indicate a normal condition and/or position of a system.
6. SCRs are used in most systems to complete a path to ground. This causes both the associated annunciator and the fault indicator to illuminate..

R3 is used to adjust the voltage output to 12 VDC, while R4 is used to balance the voltage output between generators 1 and 2.
Now pick up and analyze the PC130-737 card. This card has 4 annunciator indicators: Gen Fail, Fuel Pressure, Over Heat, and Door Open.
KEHQQSVSSV

Each system uses a sensor to trigger the annunciator circuit. PC130-737 uses two transistors (Q1 and Q8) for the Gen Fail sensor. For simplicity, the other three systems use the trainer circuits to simulate the sensors...

12 VDC from PC130-735 is applied to the LED side and system side of the transistors (Q1 and Q8). When the generator fails, the LED side, causing the transistor to conduct and provide a path to ground...
The voltage drop across the circuit causes one side of capacitor C3 to be lower and start to charge. During charging of capacitor C3, the applied voltage drops at least .6 to .75 volts.
This creates a differential voltage on two of the leads to the transistor Q4. Q4 triggers and delivers the voltage needed to trigger the two alarm LEDs and buzzer SCRs Q6 and Q7.
The SCRs Q6 and Q7 trigger, providing a path to ground for the pilot and copilot's Master Caution LED and buzzer.
KEHQQSVSSV

Once the circuit is fully activated, the voltage becomes balanced at the transistor Q4. Triggering voltage is removed from the SCRs Q6 and Q7. This allows the Master Caution LEDs and buzzer to be cleared while the faulted system's LED remains illuminated...

The SCRs, however, remain triggered until the applied voltage is removed from the circuit. This is accomplished when one of the reset switches (S1 or S2) is pressed. Momentary loss of power and no trigger voltage cause both SCRs to reset...
To reset the buzzer but not the LEDs, switch S3 is used, which affects Q6 only.

All of the system fault indicators are activated in the same way, with the exception of the one for fuel pressure. The Fuel Pressure indicator is a caution alert, triggering only the Master Caution LED's SCR via Q7...
Diode D3 prevents the triggering voltage from affecting the buzzer SCR Q6. However, the diode does allow the triggering voltage to pass to SCR Q7 from the other system transistors.
